Are the printed Decalogue cantillations grammatical?

The question

The two Decalogues (Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5) are each chanted two ways: the טעם תחתון (taxton, “lower”) division into ordinary-length verses, and the טעם עליון (elyon, “upper”) division by commandment, which makes the short prohibitions (murder, adultery, theft) their own tiny verses and folds long passages into single long ones. Issue #36 grammar-checked the Tiberian-manuscript (WLC / MAM) taxton and elyon threads by detangling WLC’s dual cantillation. This page (issue #52) asks the companion question for the printed editions (דפוסים, also Koren and Simanim): fed through the very same prose grammar checker, are their taxton and elyon accentuations grammatical too?

Unlike the manuscript thread, the printed and manuscript readings are already single cantillation, spelled out word-for-word on the Wikisource base page עשרת הדברות בסיס/טעמים. Each chanted verse (delimited by its own sof pasuq) is fed through the shared pipeline — a leading verse-start token, the prose scanner, then the prose PLY grammar — exactly as issue #36 does. The manuscript versions are the baseline (MAM’s own authoritative text, expected all clean); the printed versions are the object of study.

The verdict

Tiberian manuscriptPrinted editions
Exodus 20 — taxton (lower)✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Exodus 20 — elyon (upper)✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)
Deuteronomy 5 — taxton (lower)✓ all 12 clean✓ all 13 clean
Deuteronomy 5 — elyon (upper)✓ all 10 clean✗ 1 of 9 ungrammatical (verse 1)

taxton is grammatical everywhere — both books, both traditions. The printed taxton differs from the manuscript only in details that do not touch the accent grammar (vocalization such as תִּרְצַח vs תִּרְצָח at “you shall not murder,” and where a maqaf or ga‘ya falls), and in one verse boundary: the printed taxton ends its first verse at מבית עבדים (so it has one more verse than the manuscript, which runs the first two commandments together). Both parse clean.

elyon is grammatical in the manuscript but not in the printed editions: the printed elyon of each Decalogue has exactly one ungrammatical chanted verse — its opening one.

Why the printed elyon fails: the merged first verse

In the manuscript elyon, the first commandment אָנֹכִי … עֲבָדִים is its own chanted verse, and “you shall have no other gods …” begins the next — two separate verses, both of which parse clean. The printed editions instead merge the first two commandments into a single verse (nine chanted verses in all, against the manuscript’s ten). That one merged verse is what the grammar rejects:

אָֽנֹכִי֙ יְהֹוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הוֹצֵאתִ֩יךָ֩ מֵאֶ֨רֶץ מִצְרַ֜יִם מִבֵּ֣ית עֲבָדִ֗ים לֹ֣א יִהְיֶֽה־לְךָ֩ אֱלֹהִ֨ים אֲחֵרִ֜ים עַל־פָּנַ֗י לֹ֣א תַעֲשֶֽׂה־לְךָ֣ פֶ֣סֶל׀ וְכׇל־תְּמוּנָ֡ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּשָּׁמַ֣יִם׀ מִמַּ֡עַל וַֽאֲשֶׁר֩ בָּאָ֨רֶץ מִתַּ֜חַת וַאֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּמַּ֣יִם׀ מִתַּ֣חַת לָאָ֗רֶץ לֹֽא־תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֣ה לָהֶם֮ וְלֹ֣א תׇעׇבְדֵם֒ כִּ֣י אָֽנֹכִ֞י יְהֹוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֶ֙יךָ֙ אֵ֣ל קַנָּ֔א פֹּ֠קֵ֠ד עֲוֺ֨ן אָבֹ֧ת עַל־בָּנִ֛ים עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁ֥ים וְעַל־רִבֵּעִ֖ים לְשֹׂנְאָ֑י וְעֹ֤שֶׂה חֶ֙סֶד֙ לַאֲלָפִ֔ים לְאֹהֲבַ֖י וּלְשֹׁמְרֵ֥י מִצְוֺתָֽי׃

Its accent backbone is pashta · munax · zaqef · munax · telishaqetanna · azla · geresh · munax · revia · munax · telishaqetanna · azla · geresh · revia · munax · munax · munax · pazer · munax · munax · pazer · telishaqetanna · azla · geresh · merkha · legarmeh · munax · revia · munax · zarqa · munax · segolta · munax · gershayim · mahapakh · pashta · munax · zaqef · telishagedola · qadma · darga · tevir · merkha · tipexa · atnax · mahapakh · pashta · zaqef · tipexa · merkha · silluq. The single etnaḥta falls at לְשֹׂנְאָי, leaving an over-long first half that carries a segolta plus three separate revia domains (at עֲבָדִים, עַל־פָּנַי, and לָאָרֶץ); the prose grammar cannot build it and returns a pashta_phrase error — the same failure, at the same structural point, in both Decalogues.

The cause is the merged structure, not sheer length: Deuteronomy’s printed elyon Sabbath verse runs 55 words and parses clean, while this merged verse (51 words) does not. Keeping the two commandments as the manuscript’s two separate verses (9 and 42 words) is exactly what lets them parse.

The manuscript elyon’s own single ungrammatical verse — Deuteronomy 5:8, a WLC-specific accent bug — is unrelated; it is discussed among the ungrammatical verses. Here MAM’s manuscript elyon parses clean throughout.

A handful of wiki templates are resolved to plain pointed text (legarmeh/paseq to a paseq mark, qere for ketiv-qere, paragraph and pisqa markers dropped); the chanted verses are split at sof pasuq.
